newsitem.title: USA: Thurmond challenger focuses on Senator's age.
newsitem.headline: Thurmond challenger focuses on Senator's age.

text.p: Democratic challenger Elliott Close is using age in his bid to unseat 93-year-old Republican Sen. Strom Thurmond, the oldest member of Congress.

Close, 42, a developer and heir to the Springs Industries textiles fortune, started his TV blitz last week with commercials showing photos of Thurmond from the time he started his political career as a county official in 1928 and from today, as a wrinkled elder statesman.
"He's been part of our state for most of this century. We appreciate all he's done. But this election is about the next century, not the last one," the ad says.

The commercial includes black-and-white photographs which at first show Thurmond in his 1920s clothing and then of Thurmond today. Thurmond began his Senate career in 1954 and is bidding for a record eighth term.
Thurmond's campaign manager Tony Denny dubbed the ad a political miss since it acknowledges Thurmond's decades of service.
"It's revealing that his ad doesn't speak about any of his own qualifications since you can't talk about what you don't have," Denny said of Close's commercial.
Close, a political newcomer who has never been elected to any office, has 45 days to prove he is the better candidate to represent South Carolina.

Most political observers say it is an uphill climb -- particularly since Thurmond is refusing to debate Close and both sides have agreed to a $3 million spending cap, essentially guaranteeing the same levels of TV ads.
Democrats attribute Thurmond's refusal to debate Close to old age, while Republicans say it is intended to deny Close free advertising.

"To win a race like this against someone as strong as Thurmond, you've got to be in a position to make a splash," said Winthrop University political scientist Glenn Broach. "I don't know that Elliott Close has the personality to do it."
The most recent statewide poll, taken last month, gave Thurmond a comfortable lead, 52 percent to 38 percent, according to the Post and Courier of Charleston.
Close spent last Friday night talking to Democrats near Charleston, many of whom also pointed to Thurmond's age.
"I can't give my vote to somebody who refuses to debate the issues as we head into the 21st century," said Diane Shocky of Goose Creek.
"There is absolutely nothing more that Strom can show to us that he hasn't already shown," said Joe Jefferson of Pineville.
Bill Moore, a political scientist at the College of Charleston, said that with six weeks to go, Close needed to score a knockout and start swaying Republican voters.

"He's got to target certain groups of Republicans and make himself an acceptable alternative for Republicans," he said. "That has to be migrants who have moved into South Carolina who haven't been touched by Strom Thurmond or younger Republicans who haven't been enthralled with Strom Thurmond."
Close campaign spokeswoman Victoria Channing-Lee said that was part of the strategy, especially among anti-Newt Gingrich Republicans or those upset with the far and religious right.
"The disgruntled Republicans," she said, angry at the "extremism (the elections of) '94 brought into the Congress and into the state."
In conservative South Carolina, Close says he is running his own grass roots campaign and is shunning any help from the Clinton White House.
Meanwhile, Thurmond is calling on a long list of big-name Republicans to help out, including George and Barbara Bush, who are scheduled to visit the state Wednesday.
